findings.matters: Large central contingency holdings in Q1 indicate the council did not fully anticipate pressures at budget-setting and is now rationing access to contingency; deployment of holdings accelerates and reduces flexibility for further pressures.

findings.paper_title: Housing Capital Investment and Budget Virements
findings.headline: The council lacks adequate asset condition data and is accelerating surveys from 21% to 54% coverage in four months.
findings.detail: During 2025/26 the council recognised it must significantly accelerate its stock condition survey programme to meet Regulator expectations for 'accurate, up-to-date and evidenced understanding' of housing condition. From February to May 2026, properties with current surveys increased from 21.36% to 53.90% through procurement of additional external consultancies and deployment of in-house surveyors. The council targets 90% coverage within the calendar year, with a future target of refreshing 20% of stock annually so every home is surveyed within five years.
findings.matters: This demonstrates a significant governance and regulatory compliance gap. The Regulator of Social Housing requires evidence-based understanding of stock condition. The acceleration from 21% to 54% coverage in a single quarter indicates the council was previously not meeting this expectation, and is now in catch-up mode on a mandatory requirement.
findings.figures: 21.36% coverage Feb 2026; 53.90% by May 2026 (11,369 homes surveyed); target 90% by end-2026; total stock ~21,000 homes
findings.quote: Recognising the need for more comprehensive and up-to-date information on the condition of Council homes, work commenced this year to implement a programme of stock condition surveys that refreshes the information already held within the council's Keystone Asset Management software.

findings.paper_title: Housing Capital Investment and Budget Virements
findings.headline: Stock condition surveys identified 472 Category 1 (severe) safety hazards affecting 6.3% of surveyed homes.
findings.detail: As the council accelerated its stock condition survey programme during 2025/26, physical inspections using the HHSRS framework identified significant numbers of safety hazards. Of homes surveyed by May 2026, 6.3% contained at least one Category 1 severe hazard. Damp and mould is the most commonly identified hazard. The council reports these findings to teams for urgent remedial action, with timescales aligned to Awaab's Law requirements. The council is increasing resources, tracking and coordination between asset management, repairs and compliance teams.
findings.matters: Category 1 hazards indicate homes with serious safety failures requiring urgent remediation. The scale of discovered hazards demonstrates that the council's previous understanding of housing stock condition was significantly incomplete. These findings generate immediate compliance obligations and require capital and repairs spending.
findings.figures: 472 Category 1 (severe) hazards identified; 1,157 Category 2 (moderate); 3,082 total hazards found Feb-May 2026; 6.3% of surveyed homes have at least one Category 1 hazard
findings.quote: Where a severe hazard is identified, this is reported to the Council on the same day it is identified and is passed to an appropriate team to arrange for urgent remedial action. Timescales are aligned with current repairs target times and service level agreements, as well as the requirements of Awaab's Law.

findings.paper_title: Housing Capital Investment and Budget Virements
findings.headline: Non-decent homes increased from 1.9% to 8.72% of stock in one year.
findings.detail: Non-decency rose to 1,760 homes (8.72% of 20,188 total) in 2025/26, compared to 1.9% the previous year. The council attributes this primarily to component-level data held in its Keystone asset management system, particularly external and fabric-related elements such as wall finish, roof coverings and external doors. The council notes that affected properties are clustered by street, block or estate, suggesting some may reflect legacy data assumptions rather than current condition. Targeted validation surveys are underway to distinguish actual defects from data correction.
findings.matters: Non-decency is a regulatory measure and the primary indicator of housing stock quality. A lender needs to understand whether this movement signals actual deterioration in asset condition (requiring capital remediation) or prior data quality failures (signalling governance gaps). Either interpretation indicates that management attention and capital investment are required.
findings.quote: The reported increase in non-decency to 8.72% at year end from 1.9% for 25/26 is primarily driven by component-level data held in Keystone asset management system, particularly external and fabric-related elements, including wall finish, wall structure, roof coverings and external doors.

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management and Capital Mid-Year Update
findings.headline: Capital programme financing dependent on Strategic Asset Review delivering capital receipts
findings.detail: The council faces a capital financing deficit that will increase the underlying borrowing requirement if not offset by capital receipts. The council plans to mitigate this through capital receipts from a Strategic Asset Review. These proceeds could alternatively fund transformation programmes under the Flexible Use of Capital Receipts direction. The capital programme's financial viability depends on either asset sales proceeds or reductions in planned expenditure elsewhere.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know whether the council's financing strategy is dependent on uncertain future events. Reliance on asset sales to manage a capital funding gap creates credit and liquidity risk if the disposals do not materialise or yield less than forecast.
findings.figures: Capital programme slippage £48.35m; council states 'the rise in CFR can be mitigated in future years through the generation of both identified and unidentified capital receipts'
findings.quote: Where there is a deficit in the in-year resource position, this will result in an increase in the underlying borrowing requirement. As noted below, the rise in CFR can be mitigated in future years through the generation of both identified and unidentified capital receipts.

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management and Capital Mid-Year Update
findings.headline: £48m capital programme slippage driven by material housing delivery challenges
findings.detail: The approved 2026/27 capital programme of £293.8m is being revised down to £245.5m—a 16.4% variance of £48.35m. The majority (£47.71m) stems from the HRA housing development programme. Greenwich Builds Phase 2 Year 1 is experiencing delivery difficulties with progress slower than anticipated. £34m in HRA acquisitions remains stalled in developer negotiations. These are not routine re-profiling but explicit execution risks on housing, a stated strategic priority.
findings.matters: A lender needs assurance that a council can execute capital plans on time and on budget. A 16% mid-year slippage combined with explicit statements of delivery challenges indicates operational execution risk rather than forecasting refinement.
findings.figures: Approved budget £293.80m, revised forecast £245.45m, total variance (£48.35m); HRA Housing Development variance (£47.71m); HRA Acquisitions underspend £34m
findings.quote: HRA Acquisitions (£34m) – discussions are on-going with developers on the acquisition of new council homes, with formal agreement not yet concluded. Contract payment milestones generally include a % payment at Start on Site and Golden Brick, thus extended negotiations can result in significant slippage.

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management and Capital Mid-Year Update
findings.headline: PWLB rates forecast higher while council needs to borrow £233m in 2027/28
findings.detail: Treasury advisers have revised PWLB rate forecasts upward due to higher gilt yields and geopolitical uncertainty. Bank Rate is expected to remain at 3.75% for longer than previously anticipated. The council faces a capital financing requirement necessitating £233m of new borrowing in 2027/28, followed by £181m in 2028/29 and £108m in 2029/30. This timing creates a refinancing and cost risk as large borrowings will be needed at higher rates than previously budgeted.
findings.matters: A lender assessing creditworthiness must understand whether the council faces upward pressure on debt service costs from rising market rates coinciding with large new borrowing at higher prices than previously planned.
findings.figures: Projected new borrowing requirement £233m (27/28), £181m (28/29), £108m (29/30); 5yr PWLB forecast from 5.00% (Dec 2026) to 4.20% (Mar 2029); current debt portfolio weighted average rate 4.21%
findings.quote: The forecast for PWLB borrowing rates has increased compared with earlier projections as a result of higher gilt yields and continued geopolitical uncertainty. This may increase the cost of future borrowing in the short term and reinforces the need for careful timing of borrowing decisions.

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management and Capital Mid-Year Update

findings.detail: The council's advisors forecast Bank Rate will remain at current 3.75% levels through at least March 2027, longer than earlier expected. The MPC made no changes in its April, June and July 2026 meetings as it continues to monitor inflationary pressures.
findings.matters: Extended period of higher rates delays expected benefits of refinancing or lower investment returns; compresses timeline for cost reductions and extends period of elevated financing costs
findings.figures: Bank Rate 3.75% since March 2026; forecast to remain 3.75% through Mar 2027
findings.quote: The latest forecast from MUFG Corporate Markets indicates that Bank Rate is likely to remain at current levels for longer than previously anticipated as the MPC continues to monitor inflationary pressures.

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management and Capital Mid-Year Update

findings.detail: The council is dependent on realisation of capital receipts from Strategic Asset Review to offset capital programme deficit. Two Flexible Use of Capital Receipts bids (£1.4115m) have been approved with savings forecast to exceed cost of capital, with sufficient receipts secured to date for 2026/27.
findings.matters: Capital receipts strategy is critical to managing borrowing requirement; delays or shortfalls in asset sales would directly increase external borrowing need and debt service costs

findings.quote: The delivery of the Strategic Asset Review and realisation of capital receipts will have a positive impact on the Councils revenue position if applied against the current capital programme deficit.

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management and Capital Mid-Year Update
findings.headline: Debt portfolio composition favourable with 14-year weighted average maturity and low immediate refinancing risk, though longer-duration exposure moderates benefit of anticipated rate falls
findings.detail: The council's debt has weighted average duration of 14 years with some debt not maturing for at least 5 years, providing low short-term refinancing pressure. However, the long duration means the portfolio has moderate exposure to falling rates if that forecast materialises.
findings.matters: Long maturity profile reduces immediate refinancing risk; but means limited near-term opportunity to lock in savings if rates fall as forecast
findings.figures: Weighted average maturity 14 years (from 13.4 years); average rate 4.21%
findings.quote: The average interest rate on the debt portfolio has remained relatively low (compared to previous decades) in recent years and is currently 4.21%. The weighted average duration of the portfolio is 14 years.

findings.paper_title: Private Housing Enforcement Policy 2026 to 2029

The council acknowledges that inconsistency in collecting instalment payments has resulted in "difficulties in collecting owed penalties," and is adopting a new Civil Penalties Collection, Recovery and Instalments Policy to improve consistency and enforce robustly against non-payment.
findings.matters: A finance director needs to understand whether a planned £90,000 annual saving depends on improved collection policies, and what collection challenges existed previously.

findings.paper_title: Revenue Outturn
findings.headline: General Fund balance achieved through departmental underspends and contingency reserves, which council explicitly states are 'not sustainable'.
findings.detail: The £0.1m net underspend comprised £2.4m departmental underspend offset by £2.3m corporate overspend (driven by £4.4m treasury). The council states: 'Although the General Fund achieved a balanced outturn, the position was supported by departmental underspends, corporate income, a savings contingency and in-year expenditure controls. Continued reliance on one-off resources or reserves to fund recurring expenditure would reduce financial resilience and is not sustainable over the medium term.' The £5.2m savings contingency was essential to mitigating the £7.8m underlying shortfall.
findings.matters: A lender evaluates structural financial sustainability. Balance achieved through one-off measures (contingency, in-year spending controls, underspends) rather than structural alignment signals declining resilience. The council's own explicit statement that this is unsustainable is a forward warning.
findings.figures: £0.1m net underspend; £2.4m departmental underspend; £2.3m corporate overspend; £5.2m contingency deployed
findings.quote: Although the General Fund achieved a balanced outturn, the position was supported by departmental underspends, corporate income, a savings contingency and in-year expenditure controls. Continued reliance on one-off resources or reserves to fund recurring expenditure would reduce financial resilience and is not sustainable over the medium term.

findings.paper_title: Revenue Outturn
findings.headline: Emergency accommodation overspend of £3.05m reflects structural mismatch between cost and legally-limited income recovery.
findings.detail: Temporary Accommodation emergency accommodation and hotels overspent by £3.05m (up from £2.80m Q3). The paper explicitly identifies this as structural: 'The overspend primarily reflects the difference between the cost of externally provided accommodation and the amount recoverable, which is limited by legislation.' This is not a management failure—the Temporary Accommodation Cost Reduction Board achieved outturn within '1% of the forecast'. Despite receiving £4.6m funding in 2024/25, £4.0m was removed in 2025/26. The deficit is unfixable through operational efficiency.
findings.matters: A lender distinguishes between pressures solvable through management and structural deficits in the funding model. This £3.05m reflects legislation limiting income recovery, not overspending. Future budgets cannot assume this balances without ongoing subsidy.
findings.figures: £3.05m EOA and hotel overspend; structural gap due to legally-limited income recovery
findings.quote: Temporary Accommodation: EOA and Hotels (£3.05m Overspend) The outturn overspend was £3.05m, compared with £2.80m reported at Q3... The overspend primarily reflects the difference between the cost of externally provided accommodation and the amount recoverable, which is limited by legislation.

findings.paper_title: Revenue Outturn
findings.headline: SEND transport demand accelerating at 8.5% year-on-year growth (899 to 976 pupils), driving £1.5m overspend.
findings.detail: SEND transport overspent by £1.5m driven by 'an increase in the number of children with Education, Health and Care Plans (EHCPs), resulting in greater demand for transport services'. Pupils requiring transport grew 8.5% in one year. Over six years (2020/21 to 2025/26), total demand has grown from 767 to 850 children, with unit costs rising from £16,607 to £22,513 (35% increase). This growth occurs alongside contract price increases of 2.58% from GS Plus, suggesting demand management is failing.
findings.matters: A lender sees SEND cost pressures accelerating across the board. The 8.5% annual demand growth feeds into both transport costs and the broader High Needs Block deficit of £16.0m. The historical trend shows sustained structural cost growth.
findings.figures: £1.5m SEND transport overspend; EHCP transport demand up 8.5% (899 to 976); six-year growth from 767 to 850; unit costs up from £16,607 to £22,513

findings.headline: Children's residential placement costs rising to £7,135 per week average (up from £6,370) despite reduction in numbers from 404 to 388.

The paper identifies 'residential placement costs have increased by approximately £2.3m since the beginning of the financial year', driven by 'a growing number of children presenting with complex and challenging behaviours, leading to increased provider support requests'. This cost inflation persists even as placement numbers decline, indicating structural cost drivers outpacing efficiency gains.
findings.matters: A lender assesses whether budget pressures reflect temporary spikes or structural cost inflation. Children's placements show rising unit costs despite lower volumes, suggesting cost growth is decoupled from demand management.
findings.figures: £3.1m placements overspend; average weekly residential cost £7,135 vs £6,370 in March 2025; cost increase of £2.3m despite placement reduction

However, residential placement costs have increased by approximately £2.3m since the beginning of the financial year... The average weekly residential placement cost is £7,135, compared with £6,370 in March 2025.

findings.paper_title: Revenue Outturn
findings.headline: Dedicated Schools Grant deficit reached £18.1m with High Needs Block accounting for £16.0m, growing from £12.2m Q3 forecast.
findings.detail: The DSG deficit ballooned from £12.2m predicted in Q3 to £18.1m at outturn. The High Needs Block alone accounts for £16.0m (89% of total), driven by 'increased demand for independent SEN placements across all sectors' (£4.8m) and 'historical top up costs for special academies' (£10.2m). While the statutory override protects the General Fund until 2028, relief depends on government approval of a 'Local SEND Reform Plan' for a proposed High Needs Stability Grant, and 'Even if approved, the grant would not remove the ongoing financial risk'.
findings.matters: A lender tracks contingent liabilities. The growing DSG deficit represents a future funding obligation. Statutory protection expires in 2028, and government grant relief is uncertain and conditional. Even with relief, the underlying demand growth remains unresolved.
findings.figures: £18.1m total DSG deficit (£16.0m High Needs Block); deterioration of £5.9m from Q3 forecast of £12.2m; potential grant covers 90% subject to approval
findings.quote: The gross deficit across the Central Schools Services, High Needs and Early Years Blocks is £18.3m, comprising £1.7m, £16.0m and £0.6m respectively. This is partly offset by a £0.2m surplus within the Schools Block, resulting in a net DSG deficit of £18.1m.

findings.paper_title: Revenue Outturn
findings.headline: Unachieved savings of £8.6m, with £4.4m from delivery failures indicating structural implementation challenges.
findings.detail: Gross unachieved savings total £8.6m: £3.7m from timing issues (potentially recoverable) but £4.4m from delivery issues (not recoverable) and £0.5m no longer deliverable. Examples include £0.8m Digital Services savings failing because operational requirements and licensing inflexibility prevented reductions, and £1.3m Children's Services slippage. The £5.2m savings contingency held centrally was deployed to reduce this £7.8m net shortfall to a manageable £2.6m impact on the General Fund.
findings.matters: A lender assesses the council's ability to execute budget plans. Nearly half of unachieved savings stem from delivery failures rather than timing, suggesting structural implementation capability gaps.
findings.figures: £8.6m gross unachieved savings (£3.7m timing, £4.4m delivery issues, £0.5m no longer deliverable); £5.2m contingency required to offset

This pressure is expected to continue as internal reserves decline and external borrowing requirements increase.
findings.matters: A lender assesses future debt servicing capacity. The shift from internal to external borrowing increases the council's cost base and signals declining reserves to fund capital programmes without borrowing.

findings.quote: Treasury Management reported an overspend of £4.4m in 2025/26. Treasury Management is forecasting a £0.5m adverse variance due to increased borrowing needs and lower investment returns. This reflects the Council's capital programme continuing to require financing at a time when internal resources are constrained.
findings.matters: The shift from internal to external borrowing represents a structural change in the Council's funding position. If external interest rates remain elevated, this increases annual financing costs. It also signals reduced financial flexibility, as the Council can no longer fund capital expenditure from internal sources. This matters for future debt serviceability and capacity to respond to unexpected pressures.

findings.paper_title: 202627 Quarter 1 Revenue Monitoring Report
findings.headline: Council drawing £6.1m from reserves to support recurring budget pressures, while explicitly acknowledging this is not sustainable.
findings.detail: Total usable reserves are forecast to reduce from £205.5m to £199.4m during 2026/27 (£6.1m net drawdown). Almost all of this movement (£5.9m) relates to service earmarked reserves, falling from £78.2m to £72.3m. The General Fund balance (£18.7m) and Risk reserves (£43.8m) remain unchanged. However, the Council's finance director explicitly states: 'the use of reserves to support recurring pressures is not sustainable, as these resources can only be used once.' It flags that reserve adequacy will need reassessment as part of 2027/28 budget setting.
findings.matters: Using reserves to balance recurring pressures masks a structural deficit. Once reserves are depleted, the underlying budget pressure must be met through service cuts, income increases, or further borrowing. The Council's own finance director's statement that this is unsustainable is a clear signal that future years will require difficult decisions.
findings.figures: Total reserves reduction £6.1m (£205.5m to £199.4m); service earmarked reserves reduction £5.9m (£78.2m to £72.3m); General Fund balance stable £18.7m; Risk reserves stable £43.8m
findings.quote: the use of reserves to support recurring pressures is not sustainable, as these resources can only be used once.

findings.paper_title: 202627 Quarter 1 Revenue Monitoring Report

Housing & Safer Communities has £1.1m slippage on the £4.2m temporary accommodation savings target. Only Children's Services is on track (92% delivery).

This raises questions about whether remaining-year delivery is achievable.

findings.paper_title: 202627 Quarter 1 Revenue Monitoring Report
findings.headline: Adult social care unit costs inflating sharply despite overall activity declining, creating a £9.1m care package overspend.

Unit costs have risen significantly: residential care +12%, homecare +9%, supported living and nursing +7%. Average weekly cost for residential placements has increased by 19%, with some mental health packages up 42%. This inflation is occurring despite Q1 activity being down 3% (though still 10% above the start of 2025/26), suggesting that new placements and existing package cost increases are the drivers.
findings.matters: Care cost inflation coupled with unmet demand management targets signals a structural cost pressure that budget increases alone cannot address. The rise in unit costs outpacing general inflation suggests capacity constraints or acuity mix changes in the provider market. This trend will likely persist into future years.

findings.quote: Compared with the 2025/26 outturn, forecast expenditure has increased by 12% for residential care, 9% for homecare and 7% for supported living and nursing care.

findings.paper_title: 202627 Quarter 1 Revenue Monitoring Report

Breakdown shows timing accounts for 50% (£4.99m), but delivery failures account for 43% (£4.29m), with £0.62m assessed as no longer deliverable.
findings.matters: The 43% delivery failure rate (vs timing delays) suggests genuine capacity or scope challenges, not merely implementation delays. This raises questions about the deliverability of future-year savings plans. The central contingency is only £5.2m, insufficient to offset full slippage if it continues.

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management and Capital Mid-Year Update ARM
findings.headline: Council identifies that capital programme slippage could increase underlying borrowing requirement and that ring-fenced grants prevent offsetting pressures across schemes.

Delayed investment may also increase "additional short-term costs (i.e. additional maintenance requirements) and delays to planned benefits arising from invest to save schemes."
findings.matters: This indicates the council has limited flexibility to manage programme underspends and that slippage will feed into higher borrowing requirements in future years, reinforcing the medium-term refinancing need.

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management and Capital Mid-Year Update ARM
findings.headline: Liability Benchmark projects the council will need to undertake £233m new borrowing in 2027/28, £181m in 2028/29, and £108m in 2029/30 as capital expenditure accelerates and internal resources diminish.

findings.matters: This signals a structural shift from cash-funded capital investment to debt-funded investment, marking a change in the council's financial position and refinancing profile over the next three years.

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management and Capital Mid-Year Update ARM
findings.headline: PWLB borrowing rate forecasts revised upward due to geopolitical uncertainty, increasing the cost of the large borrowing programme the council must undertake.

findings.matters: Timing of the £233m+ borrowing need against this rate environment will directly impact future debt servicing costs, and the council's ability to execute its programme if rates remain elevated or rise further.
