findings.paper_title: Appendix 1- Draft Pension Fund Annual Report 25.26
findings.headline: Funding level improved from 103% to 118% following 2025 actuarial valuation
findings.detail: The actuarial valuation confirmed the Fund's strong financial position, with funding level increasing from 103% (2022 valuation) to 118% (2025 valuation). This improved funding position is stated to reflect strong investment performance, prudent funding management, and support of participating employers.
findings.matters: A well-funded pension scheme reduces future calls on employer contribution rates and improves the council's long-term financial position. This is directly relevant to council budget sustainability and to any lender assessing the council's fixed obligations.
findings.figures: Funding level 103% (2022) to 118% (2025); Fund value £1.75bn to £1.96bn
findings.quote: the funding level increasing from 103% to 118%, reflecting the benefits of strong investment performance, prudent funding management and the continued support of participating employers

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management and Capital Outturn 2025-26
findings.headline: Council will shift to external borrowing as internal balance sheet resources are estimated to decline
findings.detail: The council maintained an under-borrowed position in 2025/26, using cash reserves of £306.8m instead of external borrowing (CFR £1,215m vs debt £908m). The treasury strategy document states the council expects to shift emphasis to external borrowing, as balance sheet resources available to borrow against are estimated to decrease, against a background of increased capital investment for housing.
findings.matters: Declining internal resources increase dependence on PWLB and external markets at a time when the council is pursuing sustained capital investment. This affects borrowing costs, flexibility, and the council's credit profile.
findings.figures: CFR £1,214,752k; debt £907,932k; under-borrowing £306,820k
findings.quote: Moving forward, the primary focus of the Council borrowing strategy will shift to external borrowing, as the balance sheet resource available to borrow against is estimated to decrease.

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management and Capital Outturn 2025-26
findings.headline: Major capital programme delays: contractor underperformance and regulatory delays caused £28m underspend
findings.detail: The council spent £290m of a forecast £318m capital budget. Housing schemes faced specific delivery challenges: Wates completed only 400 homes versus 600 expected on SHDF Wave 2 (£3m shortfall); Westcombe Court was delayed by Building Safety Regulator approval (3 extension requests, only approved February 2026, £3m scheme); and the 1,750-home Greenwich Builds programme has ongoing acquisition negotiations pushing spend into 2026/27.
findings.matters: Housing is 74% of the capital programme and a council strategic priority. Delays signal execution risk in major schemes and defer housing supply, which drives other revenue pressures like temporary accommodation costs.
findings.figures: £290m actual vs £318m forecast (-£28m); Wates 400 homes delivered vs 600 forecast; Westcombe Court £3m delayed to 2026/27; Greenwich Builds 1,750 homes affected by ongoing negotiations
findings.quote: The impact of Wates performance on the SHDF Wave 2 programme meant they only completed 400 homes out of the expected 600 leading to a c£3m underspend. Westcombe Court had repeated delays with the Building Safety Regulator (BSR). This £3m scheme was due to mainly be delivered in 2025/26 but was only approved in February 2026 after 3 extension of time requests from BSR.

findings.paper_title: Medium Term Financial Strategy 2026/27+
findings.headline: New savings proposals of £7.1m in 2026/27 are required to balance; delivery risk is material
findings.detail: The council has identified £7.1m of new savings/income proposals to bridge the budget gap. The s151 officer notes that 'The ability to produce any further material savings, with confidence, for [future years] in such a short period, would be somewhat challenging.' This suggests savings are at risk of non-delivery, particularly given that 'in excess of £20m of demand reduction, additional income or savings activities' are embedded in the current strategy.
findings.matters: When a council is identifying large savings with tight timescales and acknowledging that delivering 'any further material savings' would be 'challenging', there is material execution risk. Non-delivery would force budget overspends or emergency council tax rises.
findings.figures: New savings proposals 2026/27: £7.1m; Total demand reduction / savings in MTFS: £20m+; Note: Council has included risk reserve of £4.5m to mitigate delivery risk
findings.quote: The ability to produce any further material savings, with confidence, for Option B in addition to the significant level already tabled, in such a short period, would be somewhat challenging.

findings.paper_title: Medium Term Financial Strategy 2026/27+
findings.headline: S151 Officer warns that budget is balanced for 2026/27 only and that reserves are at minimum
findings.detail: The s151 Chief Finance Officer's statement (section 16) notes that 'reasonable assurances can be provided in respect of 2026/27' but warns that 'The Council still has significant budget gaps over the Medium Term from 2027/28 to 2029/30.' The statement also flags that general reserves of £19m are at the 'minimum level necessary' and that multiple external risks (inflation, demand surges, economic impacts) could erode these further.
findings.matters: The s151 statement is a statutory requirement and a formal warning signal. When the CFO states reserves are at minimum and medium-term gaps are significant, this signals financial stress ahead and reduced capacity to absorb shocks.
findings.figures: General reserves: £19m (March 2025), described as 'at the minimum level necessary'; 2025/26 Q2 overspend forecast: £7.2m
findings.quote: In conclusion, reasonable assurances can be provided in respect of 2026/27. The Council still has significant budget gaps over the Medium Term from 2027/28 to 2029/30... Earmarked reserves as at March 2025 were £171m and there will have been a degree of utilisation during 2025/26.

findings.paper_title: Medium Term Financial Strategy 2026/27+
findings.headline: Inflation and demographic demand costs rising from £21.8m (2026/27) to £116.2m (2029/30)
findings.detail: The underlying cost of demand and inflation pressures is growing relentlessly. Even after the council's efficiency and demand reduction work, it must fund £21.8m of additional costs in 2026/27, rising to £116.2m by 2029/30. This is the cost of an ageing population, increasing care costs, and general inflation on contracted services.
findings.matters: This is the core budget problem that cannot be solved by efficiency alone. A lender must understand that cost pressures are structural and accelerating, while the council's capacity to cut services without statutory consequence is limited.
findings.quote: the cost of serving a growing population and inflation on our contracts and commissioned activity... Within the September 2025 MTFS, £33.1m was forecast to be required to fund inflation and demand.

findings.paper_title: Medium Term Financial Strategy 2026/27+
findings.headline: Council tax base growth decelerating sharply: only 1% annually vs historic 2,400+ properties/year
findings.detail: Historic dwelling growth (2016/17 to 2020/21) was 2,400 properties per year. Latest growth is only ~1,000 properties per year (2020/21 to 2025/26), and the year-on-year increase in rated properties was just 1,298 (1.0%) in the latest period. This is significantly below government assumptions in Core Spending Power, costing the council £2m in foregone council tax income relative to CSP expectations.
findings.matters: Council tax base growth is the only guaranteed, locally-controllable revenue source. A sharp slowdown signals that either new housing is not materializing as expected or occupancy/valuations are weak. This narrows the council's financial options.
findings.figures: Historic growth: 2,400 properties/year; Recent growth: ~1,000 properties/year (2020/21-2025/26); Latest year: 1,298 new rated properties (1.0%)
findings.quote: between 2016/17 and 2020/21 there was an average increase of properties over 2,400 a year which has now reduced to an average growth of just over 1,000 properties between 2020/21 and 2025/26. The latest annual increase in the number of properties rated by the Valuation Office Agency year on year is up 1,298 (approximately 1.0%).

findings.paper_title: Medium Term Financial Strategy 2026/27+
findings.headline: Dedicated Schools Grant in statutory deficit with SEND transfer delayed but unfunded
findings.detail: DSG overspend is £12.2m at Q3 2025/26. The government announced in the Autumn Budget that SEND funding will transfer from councils to central government from 2028/29, but the council notes that local authorities 'will be required to demonstrate that they have taken appropriate measures to minimise and/or reduce the existing deficit as a precursor' to any transfer. The government has announced funding 90% of the accumulated SEND deficit, leaving 10% with councils.
findings.matters: DSG deficits are a structural problem across English councils. Greenwich's position suggests Schools Forum pressures are not containable within current funding. The partial government settlement in 2028/29 still leaves the council holding 10% of a material cumulative deficit.
findings.figures: Q3 2025/26 DSG overspend: £12.2m; Government to fund 90% of accumulated SEND deficit from 2028/29, council to fund 10%
findings.quote: The announcement that SEND funding will become the responsibility of the Government from 2028/29 is very welcome... We will have to await final details in the new year but indications are that there will be a requirement for local authorities to demonstrate that they have taken appropriate measures to minimise and/or reduce the existing deficit as a precursor to agreeing the final resolution and transfer of responsibility.

findings.paper_title: Medium Term Financial Strategy 2026/27+
findings.headline: Temporary Accommodation demand up 25% in two years; continued supply shortages forecast
findings.detail: From September 2023 to August 2025, households presenting for temporary accommodation increased 25%. The TA Cost Reduction Programme has saved £8.7m already, but the underlying demand continues to rise. The council forecasts housing supply will be 'smaller next year than this year and smaller again in 2027/28', meaning demand management cannot solve the cost problem. 2026/27 requires £4.2m additional funding.
findings.matters: TA is a statutory duty with open-ended cost exposure. When demand rises faster than the council can build supply, costs are essentially uncontrollable in the short term. This is a leading indicator of wider housing stress.
findings.figures: 25% increase in TA households Sept 2023 - Aug 2025; £8.7m already saved; £4.2m additional required in 2026/27
findings.quote: From September 2023 to August 2025, there has been a 25% increase in the numbers of households presenting in need of temporary accommodation... These factors combined have been modelled for next year and to provide a budget neutral service would require an additional £4.2m.

findings.paper_title: Medium Term Financial Strategy 2026/27+
findings.headline: Current-year overspend of £5.6m despite spending controls; reserves at minimum
findings.detail: Q3 2025/26 shows a £5.6m General Fund overspend (down from £7.2m at Q2 following spending controls). The council is managing this by restricting spend and drawing on reserves. General reserves stand at £19m, which the s151 officer describes as 'at the minimum level necessary', leaving little buffer for further deterioration.
findings.matters: Even before the new financial year, the council is overspending and consuming reserves intended for emergencies. This reduces financial flexibility and signals stress in budget management.
findings.figures: Q3 2025/26 General Fund overspend: £5.6m; General reserves (March 2025): £19m
findings.quote: the 2025/26 outturn forecast for the General Fund is showing a projected overspend of £7.2m. Financial controls have been introduced to address this forecast position... Any further use of reserves to support the overspend could reduce the Council's General Reserve or reduce other specific earmarked reserves, thereby depriving other key areas of resources needed to deliver key outcomes.

findings.paper_title: Medium Term Financial Strategy 2026/27+
findings.headline: Recovery Grant Guarantee of £10m per year ends in 2028/29 with no certainty of continuation
findings.detail: The government's funding guarantee (which adds £12.6m to 2026/27) is explicitly time-limited to 2028/29. This £10m annual payment is essential to the council's financial position but the government has given no indication whether it will continue into 2029/30. Removing this creates a 'cliff edge' in resources.
findings.matters: A lender must factor in the risk that a material revenue stream disappears with no alternative plan confirmed. The council is already forecasting this risk by excluding the grant from 2029/30 assumptions.
findings.figures: Recovery Grant Guarantee: £12.6m in 2026/27; £10m assumed in 2028/29; £0m in 2029/30 forecast
findings.quote: The Recovery Grant Guarantee is received in each year of the three year settlement, however there is no information as to what will happen to this funding after 2028/29. This represents a significant funding risk and a potential cliff edge in resources reduction.

findings.paper_title: Medium Term Financial Strategy 2026/27+
findings.headline: Budget gaps escalate dramatically: £35m in 2027/28, £67m in 2028/29, £101m in 2029/30
findings.detail: Following a balanced 2026/27 budget, the council faces an escalating structural deficit. By 2029/30, the budget gap reaches £101m—more than double the size of the current annual budget pressures. The council acknowledges these gaps will require either additional government funding, further service reductions, or further council tax increases beyond current maximum allowable levels.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand whether the council can sustain service delivery and debt repayment through an escalating deficit. A finance director needs to know what difficult decisions lie ahead.
findings.figures: 2027/28: £35m gap; 2028/29: £67m gap; 2029/30: £101m gap (from Table 22 and section 15.2)
findings.quote: there is a residual risk that there will be an overspend in 2025/26... The MTFS has further gaps opening up to more than £101m in the next few years – opportunities to identify and deliver savings will become more challenging in each subsequent budget round

findings.paper_title: Budget and Council Tax Setting 2026/27
findings.headline: Pupil numbers declining by 2.8%, creating structural mismatch between fixed costs and revenue.
findings.detail: Pupil numbers fell from 38,732 in 2025-26 to 37,631 in 2026-27, a decline of 1,101 pupils. While this reduction was partially offset by integration of two grants into the Schools Block funding, the underlying trend shows declining demand against a fixed cost base.
findings.matters: Declining pupil numbers reduce the council's revenue base while fixed costs (buildings, staffing contracts, maintenance) remain largely fixed, creating structural budget pressure that cannot be resolved by efficiency savings alone.
findings.quote: The 2025-26 pupil number was 38,732, compared to 2026-27 pupil numbers of 37,631. The reduction of 1,101 combined with the addition of the grants has contributed to the 2.4% increase.

findings.paper_title: Budget and Council Tax Setting 2026/27
findings.headline: Schools Central Block funding continuously declining year-on-year, driving ongoing need for service reductions.
findings.detail: The schools Central Block (funding for local authority functions including planned maintenance and virtual school) experiences continuous year-on-year reductions due to historical commitments. The council is absorbing these cuts through restructuring and service termination, but the document explicitly notes this 'increases pressure upon the MTFS'.
findings.matters: Structural reductions in school funding with no end date force the council into repeated cycles of service cuts or efficiency claims that become progressively harder to deliver, amplifying broader financial strain.
findings.figures: Continuous reduction year-on-year
findings.quote: Funding for this block continually sees a reduction year on year for historical commitments. The block provides funding for local authority functions such as planned maintenance and the virtual school. This in turn increases pressure upon the MTFS.

findings.paper_title: Budget and Council Tax Setting 2026/27
findings.headline: Net Zero Climate ambition remains uncosted and unfunded, with substantial future financial impact.
findings.detail: The S151 Officer identifies the council's Net Zero Climate ambition as one of the two largest risks in the Strategic Risk Register (alongside the MTFS itself). Critically, this ambition is 'neither costed or funded', yet is expected to have 'a substantial impact on the costs incurred by the council over the coming years'. This represents a significant hidden liability with no budgeted funding.
findings.matters: An undefined but acknowledged major liability that will drive future budget pressures and cannot currently be quantified represents a material risk to the council's financial position and debt capacity.
findings.figures: Unquantified
findings.quote: Two of the largest risks in the councils Strategic Risk Register are the MTFS and the Net Zero Climate ambition – the latter is neither costed or funded and will have a substantial impact on the costs incurred by the council over the coming years.

findings.paper_title: Budget and Council Tax Setting 2026/27
findings.headline: General reserves held at the minimum level necessary, leaving no financial buffer.
findings.detail: As at March 2025, the council's unearmarked general reserve stood at only £19m, which the S151 Officer explicitly states is 'at the minimum level necessary'. This reserve is meant to cushion uneven cash flows and cover unexpected emergencies; at minimum level, the council has virtually no safety margin.
findings.matters: Minimal general reserves reduce the council's ability to manage unexpected costs or revenue shortfalls without immediate recourse to additional borrowing or service cuts. This is a structural vulnerability.
findings.quote: As at March 2025, the council held £19m in its general reserve – the unearmarked reserve to cover all unforeseen circumstances beyond those which reserves are held elsewhere. The S151 officer considers this to be at the minimum level necessary.

findings.paper_title: Budget and Council Tax Setting 2026/27
findings.headline: General Fund overrunning by £7.2m in current year despite active cost controls.
findings.detail: At Q2 2025/26 (end of September 2025), the council is forecasting a £7.2m overspend on the general fund. The paper indicates that financial controls have been introduced to address this, but the overspend suggests underlying cost pressures are exceeding budget assumptions. The paper notes 'any residual variance after taking corrective action would need to be funded by use of reserves'.
findings.matters: This demonstrates the council is struggling to keep spending within approved budgets even in the current year, raising questions about budgetary control and forecasting accuracy.
findings.quote: At Q2, the 2025/26 outturn forecast for the General Fund is showing an overspend of £7.2m.

findings.paper_title: Budget and Council Tax Setting 2026/27
findings.headline: Medium-term budget deficits exceed £101m with mounting difficulty in identifying savings.
findings.detail: Beyond 2026/27, the council's Medium Term Financial Strategy shows cumulative budget gaps exceeding £101m. The S151 Officer explicitly warns that finding savings will 'become more challenging in each subsequent budget round', indicating the council is approaching the limits of what can be cut without affecting service delivery.
findings.matters: A lender needs assurance that the council can sustain balanced budgets. Escalating deficits with no clear solution path signal structural financial instability and raise questions about the council's ability to service additional debt.
findings.figures: more than £101m
findings.quote: The MTFS has further gaps opening up to more than £101m in the next few years – opportunities to identify and deliver savings will become more challenging in each subsequent budget round

findings.paper_title: Appendix A - Savings and Income Proposals , item 13.
findings.headline: Reablement Services Review savings range from £350k to £1.1m across years, indicating high uncertainty about deliverability.
findings.detail: Proposal 10 proposes escalating savings from reablement service redesign (£350k year 1 rising to £1,100k by year 3) based on a 'comprehensive review' undertaken by the council. However, the financial schedules show low/high estimates of 350/350/725/1100 against high estimates of 350/725/1100/1100 across the four years, indicating the council itself does not know which savings will land in which year or whether the full amount is achievable. The paper does not describe the new model, caseload impacts, or staffing headcount.
findings.matters: A £1.1m saving in adult social care (a demand-led, statutory service) is material. The wide range in estimates suggests the review has not yet concluded on the final operating model or that the council recognises execution risk. Lenders will need to know how confident the council is that this lands.
findings.figures: Low estimates: £350k (yr1), £350k (yr2), £725k (yr3), £1,100k (yr4). High estimates: £350k, £725k, £1,100k, £1,100k.
findings.quote: The Royal Borough of Greenwich currently delivers a reablement service designed to help residents regain independence and reduce the need for ongoing support. To ensure the service continues to meet the needs of the community, the Council commissioned a comprehensive review of its current approach.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A - Savings and Income Proposals , item 13.
findings.headline: Better Care Fund £300k saving is dependent on NHS joint approval and involves 'reviewing how a small proportion of BCF resources are used'—scope and deliverability are undefined.
findings.detail: Proposal 13 proposes £300k annual savings from the Better Care Fund by reviewing 'how staffing is organised' and 'how funding is balanced between hospital-based and community-based support'. This fund is jointly controlled with NHS partners, and the paper acknowledges that 'changes will be considered jointly with health partners'. No specific changes are named, no NHS sign-off is recorded, and the proposal depends on securing partner agreement for what the council describes as still-under-review decisions.
findings.matters: This saving is not within the council's unilateral control. If health partners object or prioritise other uses of BCF, the £300k will not materialise. The proposal does not indicate whether NHS partners have been consulted or agreed.
findings.figures: £300k recurring from BCF review.
findings.quote: Any changes will be considered jointly with health partners and will focus on strengthening prevention, supporting people to live independently at home, and making better use of digital tools.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A - Savings and Income Proposals , item 13.
findings.headline: Registrars Service income threatened by imminent immigration law changes and legislative widening of marriage rights, with savings plan appearing inadequate.
findings.detail: Proposal 18 assumes £100k ongoing savings from the Registrars Service, but the paper explicitly identifies that 'proposed changes to legislation around immigration' are expected to affect citizenship income (which 'last year accounted for around £300k') and that 'the right to perform weddings will be widened to celebrants and not just faith leaders or council registrar staff'. The paper describes these as coming 'in 2026' but does not quantify the impact or explain how £100k in adjustment covers losses of this scale. The proposal to add ceremony planner posts is a diversification strategy but is not risk-rated.
findings.matters: The council is relying on income from a service facing known, imminent legislative headwinds that could strip out £300k+ of citizenship income. The savings target of £100k appears to be an incomplete offset, and the diversification plan (ceremony planners) has no evidence base for income delivery.
findings.figures: Citizenship income last year: £300k. Proposed saving: £100k. Threat: legislative changes to immigration and marriage rights, both coming in 2026.
findings.quote: Proposed changes to legislation around immigration is expected to affect citizenship income which last year accounted for around £300k and the right to perform weddings will be widened to celebrants and not just faith leaders or council registrar staff again hitting income.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A - Savings and Income Proposals , item 13.
findings.headline: Children's Social Care £2.09m annual saving is contingent on staff redeployment into frozen agency positions, with no contingency if redeployment fails.
findings.detail: Proposal 14 (the council's single largest saving) relies on freezing vacant posts as they arise and redeploying displaced staff into the 34 agency positions currently held in social care (as of September 2025). The paper states 'These initiatives will mitigate staff redundancies' but offers no fallback if staff cannot be redeployed or if agency numbers grow. The saving is built into the MTFS as firm (£2,090k recurring) without noting the execution risk. If redeployment stalls, the council either incurs redundancy costs or has to find replacement savings of £2.1m.
findings.matters: This is the largest single saving in the plan and depends entirely on operational execution. Children's social care is a statutory service and high-cost area. Redeployment risk is material to whether the MTFS is achievable, and lenders will want to know how exposed the council is if this fails.
findings.figures: £2,090k recurring from year 1; 34 agency staff as of September 2025 to be replaced by redeployed staff.
findings.quote: Posts are currently being frozen as vacancies arise. As of Sept 2025, there were 34 agency staff in social care. These initiatives will mitigate staff redundancies.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A - Savings and Income Proposals , item 13.
findings.headline: Digital Strategy savings plan relies on 'flexible use of alternative funding mechanisms such as capital receipts to cover resource costs'.
findings.detail: Proposal 5 proposes £600k recurring savings in the Digital Service through staffing reshape and operational budget review, but the justification text explicitly states the council will use 'capital receipts to cover resource costs for investment and change projects'. Using capital receipts (one-time money from asset sales) to fund recurring revenue costs masks the true recurring position and is not a sustainable funding method. This suggests the recurring savings may not be real, or the council is deferring the problem.
findings.matters: Capital receipts are finite and typically committed to capital investment. Using them for revenue masks a structural budget problem and leaves future years exposed when receipts dry up. A lender needs to know if £600k of the planned savings is actually just a timing transfer from capital to revenue.
findings.figures: £600k recurring savings proposed; funding approach mentions flexible use of capital receipts.
findings.quote: The proposal achieves savings through a combination of measures, including a reshaping of staffing to better align with current demand, review of operational budgets and the flexible use of alternative funding mechanisms such as capital receipts to cover resource costs for investment and change projects

findings.paper_title: Appendix A - Savings and Income Proposals , item 13.
findings.headline: Three proposals substitute council budgets with temporary government Crisis and Resilience Fund (CRF) that terminates in 2029/30, creating a £1.6m funding cliff.
findings.detail: Items 6, 7, and 8 propose substituting Emergency Support Scheme administration (£250k), ambient food provision (£150k), and welfare rights spend (£700k year 1, declining to £0 by year 4) with CRF allocation. The CRF funding is described as temporary, and the council has identified no alternative funding for the permanent baseline services these proposals replace. In year 4 (2029/30), the CRF drops away entirely for items 6 and 7, and welfare rights returns to full cost. This leaves the council having to either reinstate spending, find £1.1m of new savings, or leave residents without these services.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know whether proposed savings are sustainable or dependent on temporary government grants. If the grant ends and the council has no plan, the MTFS assumptions break. This suggests the budget may not be balanced at the end of the planning period.
findings.figures: ESS: £250k years 1–3, £0 year 4. Ambient food: £150k years 1–3, £0 year 4. Welfare Rights: £700k (year 1), £500k (year 2), £200k (year 3), £0 (year 4).
findings.quote: To substitute Emergency Support Scheme (ESS) administration spend with the Government's new Crisis and Resilience Fund (CRF)... There is no proposed reduction in service.

findings.paper_title: Housing Revenue Account Medium Term Financial Strategy & 2026/27 Budget and Rent Setting
findings.paper_url: https://committees.royalgreenwich.gov.uk/documents/s18216/Housing Revenue Account medium term financial strategy and budget and rent setting for 2026-27.pdf
findings.headline: Universal Credit managed migration caused arrears spikes in 2025/26, requiring further automation investment to resolve
findings.detail: The council's rent collection and arrears reduction programme (a key PID with £450k 2026/27 savings target) was set back by managed migration to Universal Credit, which created 'spikes in arrears due to complex cases moved over to UC from legacy benefits.' The council has deployed a 'Universal Credit rent verification robot' but is investing further in automation and technology to address the problem.
findings.matters: Rental income collection is volatile and affected by factors outside the council's control. Betting on further automation to hit £450k savings (rising to £600k by 2027/28) is risky given the recent setback. Collection rates are a leading indicator of tenant financial stress.
findings.figures: Rent collection PID target: £450k saving 2026/27, rising to £600k 2027/28-2028/29.
findings.quote: Managed migration of UC in 2025/26 has resulted in spikes in arrears due to complex cases moved over to UC from legacy benefits, but this has stabilised.

findings.paper_title: Housing Revenue Account Medium Term Financial Strategy & 2026/27 Budget and Rent Setting
findings.paper_url: https://committees.royalgreenwich.gov.uk/documents/s18216/Housing Revenue Account medium term financial strategy and budget and rent setting for 2026-27.pdf
findings.headline: Building Safety Regulator costs unknown but could reach £180k annually for five years with no funding identified
findings.detail: Greenwich has 73 high-rise blocks requiring assessment by the Building Safety Regulator. The council is 'waiting for details' of the costs. In a worst-case scenario, costs could approach £180k per year over five years. The report provides no contingency and notes this 'would not imply that there are any problems with our buildings, just that as a large urban landlord we have many high-rise blocks.'
findings.matters: A potential £900k liability (5 years × £180k) sits unquantified in the budget. This is not optional compliance; it is a statutory regulator requirement. The 'worst-case' language suggests the council is uncertain of the real cost.
findings.figures: Worst-case annual cost: £180k per year over five years (£900k total). Actual cost: unknown.
findings.quote: we are waiting for details of the Building Safety Regulator's costs for assessment of our building safety cases. In the worst-case scenario this could approach £180,000 per year over five years.

findings.paper_title: Housing Revenue Account Medium Term Financial Strategy & 2026/27 Budget and Rent Setting
findings.paper_url: https://committees.royalgreenwich.gov.uk/documents/s18216/Housing Revenue Account medium term financial strategy and budget and rent setting for 2026-27.pdf
findings.headline: HRA borrowing increasing and sensitive to interest rate rises, with council noting close review needed
findings.detail: The HRA is in a period of capital-intensive borrowing to finance new builds and major works. The report flags that the HRA 'is sensitive to changes in the public borrowing interest rate' and states 'we will keep this under close review.' The council initially planned to reduce capital spending to save £1.479m in borrowing costs but had to reverse half of that reduction, losing £917k in savings.
findings.matters: Any rise in PWLB rates will directly hit HRA finances. At current thin reserve levels, this is a material risk. The council is unable to absorb rate rises through spending cuts because safety-critical work and retrofit programmes cannot be deferred.
findings.figures: Originally planned capital rephasing: £40m (10% of £400m programme). Revised to £20m (5%). Lost savings: £917k.
findings.quote: The HRA is in a period of increased borrowing to finance capital works and new builds, and is sensitive to changes in the public borrowing interest rate. We will keep this under close review.

findings.paper_title: Housing Revenue Account Medium Term Financial Strategy & 2026/27 Budget and Rent Setting
findings.paper_url: https://committees.royalgreenwich.gov.uk/documents/s18216/Housing Revenue Account medium term financial strategy and budget and rent setting for 2026-27.pdf
findings.headline: Financial plan assumes rent convergence from 2027/28 at £1/week, but government only recently confirmed this policy and could change it
findings.detail: The budget and 10-year forecast depend on the government's policy allowing rent convergence (bringing below-formula rents up towards formula levels) from 2027/28. The government announced this policy only on 28 January 2026. The council notes that if convergence is not allowed from 2027/28, there will be a 'negative impact' on the HRA, though they believe this 'unlikely.' The plan provides no contingency.
findings.matters: The financial plan is contingent on a policy the council does not control. Government could change its mind, delay it further, or reverse it. The council provides no fallback plan and describes non-implementation as 'unlikely' without supporting analysis.
findings.figures: Potential income if convergence delayed: impact described as 'negative' but unquantified. If convergence is allowed from 2028/29 instead of 2027/28: provisional £0.850m additional income.
findings.quote: If convergence is not allowed in 2027/28 there will be a negative impact on the HRA, but we believe this is unlikely.

findings.paper_title: Housing Revenue Account Medium Term Financial Strategy & 2026/27 Budget and Rent Setting
findings.paper_url: https://committees.royalgreenwich.gov.uk/documents/s18216/Housing Revenue Account medium term financial strategy and budget and rent setting for 2026-27.pdf
findings.headline: Pension fund surplus providing only temporary £1.28m annual relief, ending by 2029/30
findings.detail: The council's pension fund is now 118% funded (better than expected). This generates £1m annual ongoing saving on contributions plus a temporary distribution of £1.28m per year, but only for the three years 2026/27-2028/29. After that, this relief disappears entirely. The financial plan is structured around this temporary benefit.
findings.matters: The HRA's financial position depends on a one-off injection that ends in three years. When it ends, the HRA will face a £1.28m annual cliff without other mitigations in place. This creates a known funding crisis in 2029/30.
findings.figures: Ongoing annual saving: £1m from 2026/27 onwards. Temporary distribution: £1.28m per year 2026/27, 2027/28, 2028/29 only.
findings.quote: a saving of £1.28m is also available to the HRA each year in 2026/27, 2027/28 and 2028/29 only, as a result of the surplus.

findings.paper_title: Housing Revenue Account Medium Term Financial Strategy & 2026/27 Budget and Rent Setting
findings.paper_url: https://committees.royalgreenwich.gov.uk/documents/s18216/Housing Revenue Account medium term financial strategy and budget and rent setting for 2026-27.pdf
findings.headline: Rising legal disrepair cases from tenants despite improving repairs performance, with council proposing £500k annual reduction
findings.detail: Despite completion rates improving and tenant satisfaction rising, the number of legal disrepair cases (where tenants sue the council over repairs failures) is nonetheless increasing. The council attributes this to lawyers being 'increasingly active' in London. They are proposing £500k annual savings to address this through earlier intervention and better case management.
findings.matters: This is a structural problem: the council's repairs service is completing work on time and tenants are more satisfied, yet legal costs are rising. This suggests a systemic issue beyond operational fixes. The £500k saving assumes intervention works, but the problem is worsening.
findings.figures: Proposed saving: £500k annually 2026/27-2029/30
findings.quote: the number of legal disrepair cases is nonetheless rising. This is not unique to Greenwich – lawyers are increasingly active in offering legal disrepair services to tenants across London. This project aims to reduce these costs by increasing efficiencies in the process at an early stage.

findings.paper_title: Housing Revenue Account Medium Term Financial Strategy & 2026/27 Budget and Rent Setting
findings.paper_url: https://committees.royalgreenwich.gov.uk/documents/s18216/Housing Revenue Account medium term financial strategy and budget and rent setting for 2026-27.pdf
findings.headline: Council is skipping normal Major Repairs Reserve provisioning in 2026/27 to balance the budget
findings.detail: Instead of making a Voluntary Revenue Provision above the Major Repairs Reserve (normal practice), the council is not provisioning anything in 2026/27. This is explicitly described as being 'to assist the HRA in achieving a balanced budget.'
findings.matters: This is a workaround to make the numbers work, not genuine financial sustainability. It shifts costs into future years and shows the council cannot balance the budget through operations alone.
findings.figures: Major Repairs Reserve Voluntary Revenue Provision: £0 in 2026/27
findings.quote: To note that a HRA Voluntary Revenue Provision on amounts above the Major Repairs Reserve will not be provided in 2026/27, to assist the HRA in achieving a balanced budget and adequate Minimum Working Balance.

findings.paper_title: Housing Revenue Account Medium Term Financial Strategy & 2026/27 Budget and Rent Setting
findings.paper_url: https://committees.royalgreenwich.gov.uk/documents/s18216/Housing Revenue Account medium term financial strategy and budget and rent setting for 2026-27.pdf
findings.headline: HRA reserves forecast to stay within £242k of minimum working balance from 2026/27 to 2028/29, severely limiting financial headroom
findings.detail: The council's reserve position shows closing balances of £4.547m (2026/27), £4.524m (2027/28), and £4.305m (2028/29) against a minimum working balance requirement of £4.305m. The 2026/27 position will peak at just £242k above the minimum. This leaves almost no buffer for adverse conditions.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know the council cannot absorb financial shocks. The council itself notes: 'the HRA is less able to respond to financial pressures. Members should be aware that difficult decisions in relation to the HRA may be needed in coming years.'
findings.figures: Closing balances: £4.547m (2026/27), £4.524m (2027/28), £4.305m (2028/29). Minimum Working Balance: £4.305m. Surplus in 2026/27: £242k.
findings.quote: The HRA is forecast to be very close to its minimum working balance requirement from 2025/26 to 2027/28, peaking at its closest at £242k surplus in 2026/27. This means the HRA is less able to respond to financial pressures.

findings.paper_title: 2025 - 2026 Quarter 3 Budget Monitor
findings.headline: Medium-term financial strategy indicates substantial funding gaps for years beyond 2026-27
findings.detail: The council's MTFS update, reported separately to Cabinet, shows substantial budget gaps in the years beyond 2026-27. The Q3 monitor does not detail these, but flags them as a risk. The council explicitly states it needs to reduce structural overspend and savings slippage in the current year to avoid those pressures worsening.
findings.matters: A lender would want to know the scale and phasing of the medium-term gaps. If they are as large as the current year's overspend, the council may face difficult decisions on service cuts, further reserves usage, or seeking additional support.
findings.figures: Not specified in Q3 monitor; described as 'substantial'
findings.quote: The update relating to the Medium Term Financial Strategy, reported to Cabinet separately on this agenda indicates a substantial funding gap for forthcoming years, as such the council will need to ensure that in the current financial year, it reduces the risk of any structural overspend or savings slippage impacting upon that period.

findings.paper_title: 2025 - 2026 Quarter 3 Budget Monitor
findings.headline: General Reserves being drawn down to cover revenue overspends; council warns this strategy is not sustainable beyond the short term
findings.detail: The forecast overspend of £5.6m on the General Fund will be met either from the General Reserves (which stand at £19m) or earmarked reserves. The council explicitly states that 'Consumption of these revenue reserves to support day to day revenue expenditure would erode the budget principle of a maintenance of reserves at a prudent level. This is not a strategy that should be relied upon in the medium to long-term.' This is the council's own assessment that it is eroding its buffer.
findings.matters: A lender would interpret this language as a warning that the council's reserves are being consumed faster than is prudent and that the council is aware it is approaching a point where it cannot continue this pattern.
findings.figures: £5.6m overspend; General Reserves £19m
findings.quote: Consumption of these revenue reserves to support day to day revenue expenditure would erode the budget principle of a maintenance of reserves at a prudent level. This is not a strategy that should be relied upon in the medium to long-term.

findings.paper_title: 2025 - 2026 Quarter 3 Budget Monitor
findings.headline: Treasury management overspend of £3.4m driven by higher interest costs on increased capital financing requirement and lower investment income
findings.detail: The council's treasury position is forecasting a £3.4m overspend. This is driven by three factors: the increased borrowing need (Capital Financing Requirement) arising from the capital programme funding deficit, lower investment returns due to forecast reductions in Bank of England interest rates, and declining internal reserve balances forcing more borrowing. This is a structural cost, not a one-off.
findings.matters: Rising treasury costs erode financial headroom. A lender would be concerned that as reserves fall and external borrowing rises, the council's interest bill will continue to grow, compressing the revenue budget further.
findings.figures: £3.4m treasury overspend forecast
findings.quote: The current treasury position is reporting an overspend of £3.4m in 2025/26. This is due to a combination of factors including an increase in the Council's Capital Financing Requirement (borrowing need) arising from the historic and projected funding deficit within the approved Capital Programme and lower investment returns due to forecast reductions in the Bank of England interest rates.

findings.paper_title: 2025 - 2026 Quarter 3 Budget Monitor
findings.headline: Council has exhausted internal borrowing capacity and is now dependent on external debt; £101m borrowed as of September, more expected
findings.detail: The council has historically used reserves to fund capital expenditure (internal borrowing) to avoid external borrowing costs. This capacity is now exhausted. As at 30 September 2025, £101m of external borrowing has been undertaken, with significantly higher levels expected before the year-end. This is a structural shift: all new capital funding and potentially some revenue pressures will now need external finance.
findings.matters: Loss of internal borrowing capacity is a key moment in a council's financial trajectory. It signals that reserves are depleted and the council is now fully exposed to gilt yields and borrowing costs. A lender would need to understand the long-term capital programme and borrowing need.
findings.figures: £101m external borrowing as at 30 September 2025; higher levels expected by year-end
findings.quote: the Council has now exhausted its internal borrowing capacity. As a result, all new borrowing must be sourced externally. As at 30 September 2025, £101m of external borrowing has been undertaken. A significantly higher level of long-term borrowing is expected before the end of the financial year, as outlined in the Treasury and Capital Mid-Year 2025–26 Report.

findings.paper_title: 2025 - 2026 Quarter 3 Budget Monitor
findings.headline: Temporary Accommodation structural overspend of £3.3m on hotels and emergency beds, despite £4m budget cut and agreed £2.2m structural target
findings.detail: The council cut the TA budget by £4m for 2025-26 to reflect expected reductions in hotel use. It agreed an MTFS structural overspend target of £2.2m. However, the current forecast is £3.3m overspend on hotels and emergency overnight accommodation alone. This means the service is now forecast to overspend the agreed target by a further £1.1m. The drivers are continued high demand and cost pressures. A review is underway to identify in-year reductions, but no solutions have been locked in.
findings.matters: TA is the fastest-growing pressure on many English councils and the largest driver of homelessness spending variance. A lender would be concerned that the council's management actions (acquisitions, direct offers, lease units) have not yet shifted the cost curve meaningfully.
findings.figures: £3.3m forecast overspend on hotels/EOA; budget cut £4m; structural target £2.2m, forecast to overspend by £1.1m on top of that
findings.quote: The TA service continues to be under both demand and cost pressures... For Hotels and Emergency Overnight Accommodation, the current forecast is a £3.3m overspend. The MTFS target spend, despite targeting a £4 million cost reduction, is £2.2m above the 25/26 budget. This structural overspend was agreed in November 2024 but the forecast is now to overspend this £2.2m target by a further £1.1m.

findings.paper_title: 2025 - 2026 Quarter 3 Budget Monitor
findings.headline: DSG statutory override expires March 2028; extension uncertain and could create serious financial risk
findings.detail: The government's statutory override allowing councils to deficit-finance DSG expires in March 2028. The document explicitly flags that if this is not extended, the council could face serious financial consequences. No alternative funding mechanism is described. The council's strategy assumes the override will be extended but has no plan if it is not.
findings.matters: This is a medium-term cliff. A lender would need to know what the council would do if forced to balance DSG in three years' time with a potential £15-20m annual structural deficit in that block.
findings.figures: Override expires March 2028
findings.quote: There is currently a DSG statutory override until March 2028. If this is not extended councils could face serious financial risks.

findings.paper_title: 2025 - 2026 Quarter 3 Budget Monitor
findings.headline: Dedicated Schools Grant overspend of £12.2m driven by 506 additional Education Health Care Plans in three years
findings.detail: The DSG (which is a ring-fenced grant) is forecasting a £12.2m deficit, up from £7.4m at Q2. The High Needs Block accounts for £11.3m of this, driven almost entirely by increased demand for EHCPs. The number of EHCPs rose from 2,446 in Jan-23 to 3,244 in Jan-25—a 21% increase in two years. The council is implementing local provision (new specialist schools and resource units) to manage the issue, but the deficit is immediate.
findings.matters: A growing DSG deficit is a live threat to the council's financial stability. Unlike other overspends, DSG is ring-fenced and cannot be cross-subsidised. The council's ability to manage it depends on whether the statutory override is extended.
findings.figures: £12.2m DSG deficit; 3,244 EHCPs in Jan-25 vs 2,446 in Jan-23 (21% increase); 506 additional plans issued
findings.quote: The increased demand for Education Health Care Plans (EHCP) across all sectors has contributed to the overspend within the HNB block.

findings.paper_title: 2025 - 2026 Quarter 3 Budget Monitor
findings.headline: £7.6m of £36.1m planned savings will not be delivered this year
findings.detail: The council budgeted £36.1m in savings for 2025-26. As at Q3, £7.6m will not be delivered: £2.7m delayed by timing issues, £4.8m by delivery problems, and £0.2m no longer possible. This means the council's structural deficit is wider than the budget assumed. Delivery issues include lack of change capacity and consultation delays; timing issues relate to policy changes requiring governance processes.
findings.matters: Undelivered savings signal the council is weaker than budgeted. A lender would see this as evidence that the council cannot execute its planned reduction programme.
findings.figures: £7.6m undelivered out of £36.1m total; £2.7m timing, £4.8m delivery, £0.2m impossible
findings.quote: Table 4 provides a further detail about the reasons why any savings are now determined to be undeliverable.

findings.paper_title: Draft Investment Strategy Statement
findings.headline: Pension fund funding level has strengthened to 118%, up from 103% in 2022, reducing council pension liability exposure
findings.detail: The Fund's improved funding position from 103% to 118% over three years indicates stronger pension asset coverage of liabilities. This 15-point improvement means the council faces reduced risk of requiring revenue contributions to top up the pension fund to meet obligations.
findings.matters: A well-funded pension scheme reduces contingent council liabilities and improves the council's financial resilience from a lender's perspective
findings.quote: The Fund's funding level has strengthened to 118% (up from 103% in 2022), providing an opportunity to refine the investment strategy while maintaining compliance with the Local Government Pension Scheme (Management and Investment of Funds) Regulations 2016.

findings.paper_title: School Place Planning and Capital Programme
findings.headline: Primary schools at serious financial viability risk with 7% pupil decline and 22% of reception places vacant
findings.detail: Primary school rolls fell 1,629 pupils (nearly 7%) in January 2025 compared with 2020. After National Offer Day 2025, 777 reception places remained vacant (22% of all capacity, ranging 7–24% across planning areas). The council has implemented two school closures (Holy Family RC 2024, Gallions Mount 2025) and multiple PAN reductions totalling 345 places (11.5 form entry) from September 2025–26. The paper warns: 'a number of schools are at serious risk of becoming financially unviable' as schools are funded on pupil numbers in the October census.
findings.matters: School funding follows pupil numbers. Declining rolls force revenue cuts or efficiency savings. Multiple schools facing unviability risk signals systemic stress affecting school sustainability and risks further closures.
findings.figures: 1,629 fewer pupils (7% decline) vs 2020; 777 vacant reception places (22% of capacity); 345 place reductions (11.5FE); 2 school closures
findings.quote: As schools are funded on the basis of pupil numbers, a number of schools are at serious risk of becoming financially unviable.

findings.paper_title: School Place Planning and Capital Programme
findings.headline: Zero Basic Needs capital funding allocated for 2025/26 through March 2028, removing main school place investment stream
findings.detail: Basic Needs was the principal capital funding for school place development, allocated annually. For 2025/26 to 2027/28, Greenwich's allocation is £NIL. Only High Needs Provision Capital Allocation remains (£3,948,641 for 2025/26). Mainstream school place investment must now come entirely from developer contributions via Section 106 and Community Infrastructure Levy, with no central government top-up.
findings.matters: Loss of Basic Needs removes the main flexible capital source for school provision. Future investment depends on developer contributions, which are unpredictable and may not align with place-planning need.
findings.figures: Basic Needs Allocation for 2025/26–2027/28: £NIL; HNPCA 2025/26: £3,948,641
findings.quote: the Council will not receive any further Basic Needs Funding for the period to 31 March 2028.

findings.paper_title: School Place Planning and Capital Programme
findings.headline: Out-of-borough SEND placements for 19–25 year-olds increased 80% in five years with significant further cost escalation forecast
findings.detail: Over the last five years, Royal Greenwich residents aged 19–25 with EHCPs increased 80%, with specialist provision increasing 54%. Over 200 young people are currently placed outside the borough. The council forecasts: 'The demand and cost for these places is expected to increase significantly over the next few years as more young people remain in education.' Out-of-borough placements carry both high placement costs and transport costs the council cannot easily control.
findings.matters: Out-of-borough SEND placements are a cost the council cannot control. An 80% five-year increase shows this is not temporary. Forecast cost escalation adds to overall budget pressure.
findings.figures: 80% increase in 19–25 year-olds with EHCP over five years; 54% increase in specialist provision requirement; over 200 currently placed out of borough
findings.quote: The demand and cost for these places is expected to increase significantly over the next few years as more young people remain in education.

findings.paper_title: School Place Planning and Capital Programme
findings.headline: High Needs Block revenue budget facing substantial financial pressures from rising EHCP numbers and extended duty to age 25
findings.detail: The paper states High Needs Block Top Up Fees 'continue to face substantial financial pressures'. Drivers include: EHCP numbers forecast to increase by over 1,400 over the next five years, increasing complexity of needs, and 'extension of the local authority's duty towards young people with SEND up to age 25'. The proportion of the 0–25 population with EHCPs now exceeds 3%, and approximately 23% of all school pupils have some level of SEND.
findings.matters: High Needs Block is a major revenue pressure for councils. EHCP numbers and complexity are outside council control but drive mandatory spending. Extended age duty to 25 increases cost exposure.
findings.figures: EHCPs expected to increase by over 1,400 over five years; over 3% of 0–25 population have EHCP; 23% of overall school population has some level of SEND
findings.quote: In respect of revenue costs, both General Fund Transport and Dedicated Schools Grant (i.e. High Needs Block Top Up Fees) continue to face substantial financial pressures.

findings.paper_title: School Place Planning and Capital Programme
findings.headline: Rowan Wood primary SEND school delivery delayed from 2026 to 2029, creating acknowledged ongoing financial risk
findings.detail: The primary phase of the Rowan Wood all-through SEND school for autism was originally targeted for September 2026. The council has now confirmed this is 'no longer feasible' and revised delivery to September 2029 – a three-year delay. The paper explicitly states this delay 'will continue to exacerbate an ongoing financial risk to Royal Greenwich due to the shortage of specialist primary places locally'. The delay extends reliance on expensive out-of-borough SEND placements.
findings.matters: The council has explicitly identified this delay as creating financial risk. Local shortage forces out-of-borough placements at higher cost. A three-year extension of this shortage multiplies the cost impact.
findings.figures: 3-year delivery delay (2026 to 2029); £24m investment envelope approved; 112 primary places planned
findings.quote: this and any further delay will continue to exacerbate an ongoing financial risk to Royal Greenwich due to the shortage of specialist primary places locally for children who need to be placed in a special school.

news_drafts.headline: Greenwich misses nearly a quarter of planned savings, with delivery problems outweighing timing delays
news_drafts.lead: Greenwich has failed to deliver nearly a quarter of its £43.5m planned savings for 2026/27, with structural delivery failures accounting for more of the gap than timing slips. The council forecasts £33.6m of savings will materialise, leaving £9.9m unachieved. Of this shortfall, £4.3m (43 per cent) stems from initiatives proving harder to deliver than expected, while £5.0m (50 per cent) relates to timing delays expected to recover later. The shortfall comes amid mounting pressure on day-to-day budgets: adult social care unit costs have risen 12 per cent on residential placements and up to 42 per cent on some mental health packages; plans for children with special educational needs have grown from 3,626 to 4,060, creating a £27.0m deficit on school funding; and demand management programmes are delivering only 74 per cent of target. The council is drawing £6.1m from reserves to support recurring pressures, a step its finance director says "is not sustainable".

news_drafts.headline: Greenwich Council repays £51m debt while planning shift to major borrowing
news_drafts.lead: Greenwich Council repaid £51 million in government loans (Public Works Loan Board debt) in the first four months of this financial year, continuing to reduce its borrowing costs by using its own cash reserves instead of taking new loans. However, the council's treasury management update shows this strategy is running out of runway. The council projects it will need to borrow £233 million in the 2027/28 financial year, followed by £181 million and £108 million in the two years after — a marked shift from its current position of having more cash than it needs to cover its long-term commitments. The timing of that borrowing matters: interest rate forecasts have risen due to global uncertainties, which will increase the cost of future loans. The council has made no new borrowing so far this year, concentrating its decisions into the final quarter, when rates may be higher.
news_drafts.paper_title: Treasury Management and Capital Mid-Year Update

news_drafts.headline: Greenwich to borrow £522m over three years as interest rates rise, council warns
news_drafts.lead: Greenwich has repaid £51m of government debt in the first four months of this financial year but faces significantly higher borrowing costs ahead. The council approved borrowing of up to £116m but has undertaken none so far, waiting for better terms. However, forecasts show it will need to borrow £233m in 2027/28, £181m in 2028/29 and £108m in 2029/30 as its capital programme accelerates. Interest rate advisors have revised forecasts upward due to geopolitical uncertainty, with five-year Public Works Loan Board rates now expected to reach 5 per cent in December before falling to 4.2 per cent by March 2028. The council's audit panel heard that careful timing of borrowing decisions will be needed to manage costs, though the underlying debt requirement—the total amount the council has spent on long-lived assets not yet paid for—is projected to peak in 2029/30.
news_drafts.paper_title: Treasury Management and Capital Mid-Year Update ARM
